scope: Defence and security procurement and industry at Union level: DAC approvals and MoD contracts as PIB names them (an `award` claim only where PIB names the vendor and the ₹ crore; joint totals, AoNs and unpriced contracts are facts on the buyer with the void 'vendor not named' or 'amount not stated'); DPSU and private production, exports and licences by year from the DDP tables and PIB; the licensed private producers (L&T, Bharat Forge, Solar Industries/EEL, Mahindra, Tata Advanced Systems, Adani Defence and PLR Systems, Data Patterns, Zen, Astra, Paras, MTAR) and Reliance Naval's NCLT outcome; offsets, the Dassault-Reliance JV and the 2016 Rafale contract; the two defence corridors and iDEX; SIPRI import shares. Three levels of resolution: Union money resolves to the line item; state money resolves to the Police major head per state (and prisons per state from NCRB), with strength and per-capita figures `reported:` while BPR&D is down; city money does not exist outside Delhi Police, and city strength has no primary while BPR&D is down — cities get the footprint (installations, commissionerate entities with `reported:` strength) and the void. This file touches only the Union procurement and industry level; it carries no state or city money. It leaves out unannounced procurement, deployments and orders of battle, and carries no budget or strength series.

PIB 2019-11-20: the Government told Lok Sabha that CAG found the package price 2.86% lower than the audit-aligned price and that 'Indian Government has not recommended any company for making Rafale jets for India' [documented]

narratives.strongestCase: Adani Enterprises has built a defence business (ADSTL / Adani Defence & Aerospace) quickly: a 51% holding in PLR Systems (reported), a 500-acre ammunition complex at Kanpur inside the UP Defence Industrial Corridor, a Hyderabad UAV and missile complex, an 85.8% purchase of Air Works (enterprise value ₹400 crore, announced 2024-12-23), and two PIB-named contracts with Adani-linked vendors: the 2025-12-30 CQB carbine (₹2,770 crore jointly with Bharat Forge, over 4.25 lakh carbines; reported split 60/40 — Bharat Forge L1, Adani/PLR L2) and the 2026-07-22 DRDO-CABS contract with ADSTL as Development cum Production Partner for AEW&C Mk-II mission systems (sole vendor for that role, amount not stated, PIB PRID 2288009). The AEL AR 2025 page records deliveries of Drishti-10 UAVs and UAV-launched precision-guided missiles to the services and a counter-drone system to the BSF, with values not published. A Gwalior small-arms maker winning part of a first-of-its-kind carbine buy, in a group that already holds ports, airports and power, is the visible core of the narrative. Per-vendor splits are not in PIB (reported 60/40 in trade press); PIB describes the whole Rs 2,770 crore as one pair of contracts.
narratives.strongestCounter: On the published record the share is small and shared: ₹2,770 crore jointly with Bharat Forge is 0.68% of this file's ₹4.07 lakh crore sample of 45 PIB-named award claims, calendar 2021-25 (≈ 0.27% at the reported 40% share; the PIB universe is larger — FY2025-26 capital contracts to 30 Dec alone were ₹1,82,492 crore per PRID 2209832), against L&T's ₹24,985 crore as sole vendor (6.1%) and Tata Advanced Systems' ₹6,900 crore joint plus the C-295 consortium; DPSUs hold 77% of the sample (HAL alone 58%). No priced sole-vendor MoD capital acquisition to an Adani entity appears in the sample; the AEW&C DcPP contract is sole-vendor but unpriced and a DRDO development partnership rather than a capital buy; the AEL AR 2025 lists deliveries of ULPGMs, UAVs, Drishti-10, SAMs and NGARM to the services and a counter-drone system to the BSF with values not published, so their scale cannot be scored. The carbine contract also names a second private vendor, and DRDO-ARDE/competitive trials are the usual route (not verified here).
narratives.whatWouldChange: A PIB or exchange-filing record of a large single-vendor award to ADSTL/PLR/Air Works (the reported carbine split puts PLR below Bharat Forge, 40/60); DAC AoNs for Adani-made items (loiter munitions, UAVs) followed by contracts without competition; the DPIIT company-wise licence list; bids data (CPPP/GeM) showing single-bid awards; electoral-bond data for defence vendors (gap, not collected). A priced follow-on to the AEW&C Mk-II DcPP contract, or any MoD disclosure of the ₹ value of the AR-listed deliveries.

narratives.claim: The Rafale offset was steered to Reliance (Anil Ambani's group) by the Government.
narratives.strongestCase: Reliance Aerostructure Ltd (the Reliance entity named in the Supreme Court judgment) 'had come into being only on 24th April, 2015' — two weeks after the 10 April 2015 Paris announcement — as the Court cites the petitioners' submission, which it accepted as a company formed 'in the recent past' (the CIN/MCA record was not opened — gap); the former French President was quoted in 2018 as saying 'The Indian government proposed this service group and Dassault negotiated with Ambani'; the offset is 50% of the contract against a policy floor of 30% (Scroll 2020-09-24); the Hollande quote and the Mediapart-reported Dassault internal document are the case for: Mediapart (Oct 2018, as relayed by ThePrint 2018-10-11) reported that Dassault deputy CEO Loïk Segalen told staff representatives on 2017-05-11 that 'it was imperative and mandatory for Dassault Aviation to accept this counterpart, in order to get the export contract from India' [reported] — Dassault's contra: it 'freely chosen' Reliance and the remark concerned the offsets (ThePrint). The CAG 2020 offsets audit found Dassault/MBDA had not confirmed ToT to DRDO (the 30% share) but found no discrepancy in the 20% private allocation that (per HT, via Scroll) includes DRAL (a Dassault-Reliance JV, February 2017).
narratives.strongestCounter: The offset guidelines (clause 4.3, quoted by the Court) let the vendor pick its Indian partner, and Dassault says 'This is Dassault Aviation's choice' while the French government said it was 'in no manner involved'; Hollande himself, asked by AFP (Sep 2018) whether India had pressured Dassault and Reliance, said he was 'unaware' and 'only Dassault can comment on this' (Scroll 2018-09-23); DRAL is about 10% of the offsets by Dassault's CEO (about a hundred partners in negotiation); the Supreme Court on 2018-12-14 found no 'substantial material ... of commercial favouritism ... as the option to choose the IOP does not rest with the Indian Government', and dismissed review on 2019-11-14; CAG Report 3 of 2019 found the price 2.86% below the audit-aligned price and does not name Reliance or DRAL; the 2020 offsets audit found no discrepancy in the 20% private allocation; in 2025 Dassault agreed to take 51% of DRAL (ThePrint/Business Standard 2025-09-05; completion unconfirmed). Anil Ambani's group is not Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries.
narratives.whatWouldChange: The French PNF judicial investigation (opened 2021 after the Sherpa complaint — The Wire 2026-02-23; the 14 June 2021 date was not confirmed in an opened source) has no published outcome; Mediapart reported (The Wire 2023-12-14) that India had de facto not executed the French judges' November 2022 request for judicial cooperation [reported]. Also: MoD offset-claim verification for DRAL; Dassault's offset-discharge statements (annual reports); any record that the Indian side shortlisted Reliance before Dassault chose it. The steering claim itself stays a narrative: no predicate in the fleet vocabulary expresses 'steered', so it is not carried as an alleged edge; the contras (Dassault, the French government, the Supreme Court) are recorded here.

narratives.claim: Make in India has not reduced imports.
narratives.strongestCase: India was still the world's second-largest arms importer in every SIPRI period since 2010-14; its import volume fell −32% (2010-14 → 2015-19), −9.3% (2015-19 → 2020-24) and −4.0% (2016-20 → 2021-25; overlapping windows, not cumulative), and its world share went 14% (2010-14) → 9.2% (2015-19) → 8.3% (2020-24) → 8.2% (2021-25); SIPRI says its 'recent orders or planned orders — including up to 140 combat aircraft from France and 6 submarines from Germany — indicate its continued and probably increasing reliance on foreign suppliers', a signed IGA (26 Rafale-Marine, 2025-04-28) and AoNs, which are not orders (MRFA Rafale and P-8I, 2026-02-12 — the ministry says the majority of the MRFA aircraft are to be manufactured in India), plus a US$ MQ-9B deal, sit in the pipeline, and flagship 'indigenous' aircraft carry foreign engines (113 GE F404 for the 97 LCA Mk1A; AL-31FP made under licence from the Russian OEM).
narratives.strongestCounter: The supplier mix and the domestic share have moved: Russia's share of India's imports fell from 72% (2010-14) to 36% (2020-24) and 70% to 40% on the later fact sheet; domestic industry took 81% of FY2024-25 contract value (₹1,68,922 crore of ₹2,09,050 crore) and 92% by count; production rose from ₹43,746 crore (2013-14) to ₹1.78 lakh crore (2025-26) and exports from ₹686 crore to ₹38,424 crore; PIB asserts 'at least 65%' of equipment is now made domestically (no method printed). SIPRI itself attributes the decline in part to India's growing ability to design and produce. Imports are measured in volume of major weapons, not rupees. Status split: the past-tense claim ('has not reduced imports') is unsupported on SIPRI volume — a decline in all three comparisons, part of which SIPRI attributes to domestic production; the forward-looking claim ('will not') is contested, SIPRI 2026 expecting 'continued and probably increasing reliance on foreign suppliers'. The file's single status field carries 'contested' for the whole. PIB's 81% is ₹ contract value signed and SIPRI's figure is TIV deliveries: not commensurable, and 'domestic industry' contracts carry imported content (GE F404 in LCA Mk1A). Control: the volume decline does not single out the policy — Pakistan −39% (2010-14 → 2015-19) and Saudi Arabia −41% (2015-19 → 2020-24) fell too, though Pakistan then rose +61% (2015-19 → 2020-24) and +66% (2016-20 → 2021-25); UPA-II-era deliveries (2010-14: 14% world share, Russia 72% of India's imports) sit beside the NDA periods above.
narratives.whatWouldChange: MoD/DGCIS import values by year; SIPRI's annual TIV for 2026-27 deliveries (Rafale-M, Scorpene follow-ons); the domestic-versus-foreign split of FY2025-26's ₹2.28 lakh crore of contracts and the foreign content of 'indigenous' contracts.

narratives.strongestCase: DPSUs plus the ex-OFB companies produced 73.8% of Indian defence output in 2023-24 (MoD AR 2024-25 table; 70.8% in 2019-20), and 'DPSUs and other PSUs' about 76% in 2025-26 (PIB 2273824); 77% of the ₹4.07 lakh crore of PIB-named awards sampled in this file, 2021-25 (45 contracts; HAL 58%) went to DPSUs — a sample, not the universe; HAL's big awards are for platforms it designs (LCA, LCH, ALH, Su-30 under licence), the DPSUs have their own Positive Indigenisation Lists (five lists, 5,012 items; 3,025 indigenised), and PIB prints no bid counts for the large DPSU contracts. The private share of production was about 20-21% from 2019-20 to 2023-24 — it did not rise across five years. Mechanism: nomination-basis awards — the CVC's April 2021 memo said 'the award of contracts/projects/procurements on nomination basis without adequate justification amounts to restrictive practice eliminating competition, fairness and equity', and private-industry executives told Defense News (2022-08-08) that nomination orders to state-run companies should stop where the private sector can compete [reported].
narratives.strongestCounter: Private firms won categories DPSUs had held: ATAGS ('first major procurement of towed guns from the private sector'), K9 VAJRA-T, the High-Power Radar ('first ... built by the private sector'), CIWS, the CQB carbine; the private share of production reached 22-24% in 2024-26 (the FY2024-25 figure was restated from 23% to 22% as the total moved to ₹1.54 lakh crore); DPSUs pass value to private suppliers (Akash: 'around 60%' of the contract); private firms took 64.5% of FY2024-25 exports; ordnance factories were corporatised into seven companies; the PIB reports 177 of 193 FY2024-25 contracts to domestic industry without a DPSU/private split. Single-source awards to the designer of a platform are protection of a kind but are not evidence of insulation from competition by themselves. Symmetry: K9 VAJRA-T 2024 is a repeat Buy (Indian) order to the private incumbent L&T (PIB 2024-12-20), so single-source repeat orders are not a DPSU-only pattern. The AMCA prototype programme: ThePrint (2026-02-04) reports HAL out of the ₹15,000 crore project, with the TATA group, a Bharat Forge-led consortium (BEML, Data Patterns) and an L&T-led consortium (BEL, Dynamatics) in the race [reported].

symmetryCheck: Vendors: the same fields were computed for every private vendor and for the DPSU in the same category. PIB-named MoD award value 2021-25 (sample of PIB-named releases; joint contracts counted once): DPSUs 77.2% (HAL 58.1%), private Indian vendors 8.7% (L&T ₹24,984.65 crore sole-vendor, 6.1%; Bharat Forge/TASL ₹6,900 crore joint, 1.7%; Bharat Forge/PLR (Adani Defence 51%) ₹2,770 crore joint, 0.68%), the BrahMos JV 5.5%, foreign vendors 5.4%, other PSU 0.7%, a Pinaka EEL/MIL mixed contract 2.5%. Adani Defence beside L&T and Tata Advanced Systems: Adani-linked vendors have no priced sole-vendor PIB-named award, one joint one (reported 40% share as L2) and one unpriced sole-vendor DRDO development-cum-production partnership (AEW&C Mk-II, 2026-07-22); L&T has five sole-vendor awards over 2022-24 including the K9 guns, CIWS and radar; TASL has the 6x6 vehicle half of a joint award and the C-295 consortium role. The identical lens run on DPSUs and on the private vendors returns the same pattern — a few mega-contracts to the platform designer dominate — which is a finding about the lens (concentration by platform design), not about any vendor. Where a DPSU and a private vendor sit on one contract (Pinaka: EEL beside Munitions India) or one category (radars: L&T beside BEL; vessels: L&T and Chowgule beside Goa Shipyard/GRSE/Cochin/HSL; artillery: L&T, Bharat Forge, TASL beside the ordnance successors), the PIB gives joint totals and no bid counts, so no head-to-head can be scored. Private share of production was 19-21% for five years (2019-24) then 22-24%; the private share of exports fell from 72% to 45% as DPSU exports rose from ₹5,874 crore to ₹21,071 crore. Union: UPA-II (FY2009-10 to 2013-14) versus NDA (FY2014-15 to 2025-26) on production, exports and imports: production ₹43,746 crore in 2013-14 against ₹46,429 crore (2014-15) to ₹1.78 lakh crore (2025-26); exports ₹686 crore (2013-14) to ₹38,424 crore; licences 215 (2014) to 788; SIPRI import share 9.1-9.3% (2015-20) to 8.2-8.3% (2020-25); the UPA-II end-year series for production and licences by year was not collected (gap), so growth rates across the two governments are only partly comparable. Cases: Rafale beside Bofors on identical fields — contract date (2016-09-23 against 1986-03-24), value and conversion (€7.87 billion ≈ ₹59,000 crore implied ₹74.96/€ against US$285 million / about ₹1,500 crore in the Bofors record of the money-people file), vendor and intermediaries named, first allegation (2018 Hollande quote against Swedish Radio 1987), investigating body (none appointed for Rafale; CBI for Bofors), courts' outcomes (SC 2018 and 2019 dismissed; Delhi HC 2004/2005 quashed, SC 2018 and 2026 dismissed), the counter-record (CAG: 2.86% below the audit-aligned price; no Indian court or audit found payment to a public servant in either) — the fields line up and neither case produced a conviction; AgustaWestland beside Tatra is carried in money-people.json and literature.json and was not repeated. Bonds: not collected (void). Imports control (SIPRI volume): India −32% / −9.3% / −4.0% across the three windows beside Pakistan −39% (2010-14 → 2015-19) then +61% and +66%, and Saudi Arabia −41% (2015-19 → 2020-24) — the decline is not unique to India, nor is it uniform among importers; UPA-II-era deliveries (2010-14: 14% world share, Russia 72%) sit beside the NDA windows.
